title: Console usage access proxy: attribute resolution + query-time authorizer
creator: Asha Kapoor
description:
Problem statement:
Console usage endpoints currently rely on a brittle mix of ad-hoc query filters and frontend-based entitlements. This causes inconsistent visibility (customers sometimes see metrics for unrelated routes), expensive database scans when tenant scopes are missing, and frequent rollbacks during releases.

Goal:
Build a stable, query-time authorization proxy for console analytics that resolves entitlements and attribute-based scopes before queries reach the analytics pipeline. The proxy must: (1) resolve role/entitlement + attribute mappings (team, product, route, token) with a local fast cache, (2) emit a normalized scope token that downstream services (metrics aggregator, exports) can consume, (3) enforce row-level restrictions in query rewriters to avoid full-table scans, and (4) fall back to a low-privilege default instead of returning full datasets.

Deliverables:
- An access-proxy service that sits between the console API and analytics query layer (gRPC + HTTP gateway).
- Attribute resolution module that merges entitlements from primary RBAC service, temporary grants (support/admin), and token-level metadata.
- Query-time authorizer that rewrites & annotates incoming SQL/DSL to include safe tenant filters or denies the request.
- L1 cache with eviction tuned for heavy-read dashboards (TTL + LRU hints).
- Integration tests with synthetic dashboards and cost regression checks.

Design trade-offs considered:
- Strongly consistent entitlement fetch vs cached eventual-consistency: chosen default is cached with a short TTL (30s) + invalidation on entitlement changes to avoid latency spikes during peak dashboard load.
- Where to enforce restrictions: rewriting queries at the proxy reduces blast radius but adds complexity; delegated enforcement to the analytics engine would require opt-in changes across multiple services. We selected proxy rewrite to centralize logic.
- Fail-open vs fail-closed: fail-closed chosen for customer-facing auditability (deny access rather than reveal too much). Internal monitoring will raise immediate alerts on denials to catch misconfigurations.

Implementation notes:
- Use existing entitlement graph exports (ENG-41207) as canonical source; reconcile with token grants service (ENG-33001).
- Cache layer: Redis cluster with per-tenant key namespaces; include a lightweight bloom filter for negative cache to reduce backend hits.
- Query rewriting patterns: parameterized route_filter clauses (route_id IN (...)), attribute masks for derived metrics, and safe aggregation fallbacks (e.g., aggregate over allowed scope only).
- Metrics: cache hit ratio, authorization latency p50/p95, denied-request rate, total query cost delta. Add cost regression alert if average scan size increases by >20%.

Acceptance criteria:
1) End-to-end request from console dashboard to analytics returns only allowed rows for synthetic test tenants used in QA.
2) Authorization latency (proxy add) p95 < 20ms in prod-like load.
3) No increase in tail query time (>10%) on representative dashboards.
4) Automated invalidation event from entitlement service causes updated scope within 30s.

Links and artifacts:
- PRD: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/ANALYTICS/Console+Usage+Access+Proxy
- Design mock: https://drive.redwood.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c_console_access_proxy
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/5627
- Dashboard (canary): https://grafana.redwood.com/d/usage-access/proxy-canary

Next steps (this sprint):
- Wire the proxy to entitlement export (ENG-41207) and implement short-TTL cache.
- Create integration tests that simulate support temporary grants.
- Load-test proxy at 10x dashboard read QPS and iterate cache eviction.

Potential follow-ups:
- Move enforcement into the query engine for advanced pre-aggregation optimizations.
- Expose a scoped token for downstream services to avoid repeated resolution work.
